entities.summary:
The Battle of the Trebia was the first major clash between the Roman Republic and Carthaginian forces in the Second Punic War, fought on December 21, 217 BCE, in the vicinity of Piacenza, Italy. This pivotal engagement saw the Carthaginians, led by General Hannibal, emerge victorious against a numerically superior Roman army, but ultimately failed to secure a decisive victory, allowing the war to drag on for another 15 years.

The consequences of the Battle of the Trebia were far-reaching, as it showcased the tactical prowess of Hannibal, who would continue to outmaneuver the Romans in the following years, culminating in the decisive victories at Cannae and Lake Trasimene. The battle also highlighted the strengths and weaknesses of Roman legionary tactics, leading to significant reforms in the Roman military.

The legacy of the Battle of the Trebia can be seen in the shifting balance of power in the Mediterranean, as the Carthaginians continued to pose a significant threat to Roman dominance, forcing the Romans to adapt and innovate in their military strategies. This, in turn, contributed to the eventual collapse of the Carthaginian empire and the rise of Rome as the dominant world power.

The battle's impact can be seen in the words of Polybius, a Greek historian who witnessed the battle: "The Romans, although they had lost the battle, were not defeated in their spirits, but, on the contrary, they were filled with a desire for revenge and a determination to win back their honor."
